explanations.answer: The signs and wonders the Most High did for him
explanations.explanation: That's it. Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, writes, “I am pleased to declare the signs and wonders that the Most High God has performed for me.” Look at whose work he's reporting. It's the Most High's, and the king isn't taking a bow for any of it.

explanations.answer: The great victories his armies have won in battle
explanations.explanation: The message never brings up his armies. He says he is pleased to declare “the signs and wonders that the Most High God has performed for me.” A king with a whole empire could have led with his battle record, and he leads with what the Most High did. I would have been tempted to open with my batch count.

explanations.answer: The plans for the next golden statue he will build
explanations.explanation: No blueprints in this letter, friend. This is a testimony, and the king says he is pleased to declare “the signs and wonders that the Most High God has performed for me.” Then in the very next verse he says, “How great are His signs, how mighty His wonders!” (Daniel 4:3).

True. The king says of the Most High, “His kingdom is an eternal kingdom; His dominion endures from generation to generation.” That's a man who runs a huge kingdom himself, calling someone else's kingdom the one that lasts. I'd say that's a good line to put at the top of a letter.

It's actually true. Nebuchadnezzar says of the Most High, “His kingdom is an eternal kingdom; His dominion endures from generation to generation.” He says it right at the start of his message, before he tells any of the story. The praise comes first, and the dream comes after.

Yes, frightened. The king says, “I had a dream, and it frightened me; while I was in my bed, the images and visions in my mind alarmed me.” He went to bed at ease and woke up rattled. Nobody walks away from a dream like that saying, "Well, that was nice."

Rested would be nice, but that's not what the text says. The king says the dream “frightened” him, and the visions in his mind “alarmed” him. He was lying in his own bed, and it still didn't help. I think I've had a few nights like that myself.

Inspired is a cheerful guess, but the king doesn't say it. He says, “I had a dream, and it frightened me,” and that the visions “alarmed” him. That's why he goes looking for someone to interpret it. A man who feels inspired doesn't usually call in every wise man in the kingdom.

Not quite. The king says, “I told them the dream, but they could not interpret it for me.” That's the magicians, enchanters, astrologers and diviners all together. Four kinds of experts walked in, and not one of them had an answer.

False, and you read it right. The king says that when he told them the dream, “they could not interpret it for me.” A whole room of magicians, enchanters, astrologers and diviners came up empty. That's a long line of experts with nothing to say.

explanations.answer: The spirit of the holy gods
explanations.explanation: That's what he says. The king tells Daniel, “I know that the spirit of the holy gods is in you and that no mystery baffles you.” Those are the king's own words about Daniel. He sees something in him that he didn't see in anyone else in the room.

explanations.answer: The wisdom of all of Babylon
explanations.explanation: The king doesn't say that. He tells Daniel, “I know that the spirit of the holy gods is in you and that no mystery baffles you.” He had just watched Babylon's wise men fail, so I think he wasn't looking for more of the same. He's pointing at something in Daniel himself.

Ancient kings never come up. The king says, “I know that the spirit of the holy gods is in you and that no mystery baffles you.” That's what he sees in Daniel, and it's why he hands him the dream. It's a short compliment with a very big job attached.
Shelter is right. The king says, “Under it the beasts of the field found shelter.” That's a tree big enough that the animals just move in under it. I'd like a cookie jar that popular.
Yes, fed. The king says “from it every creature was fed,” and that “upon it was food for all.” This tree wasn't just tall, it was taking care of everybody. Birds nested in its branches too.

Danger isn't in the dream's picture of the tree. The king says the beasts of the field “found shelter” under it. Nobody was running away from this tree until later, when the watcher calls out for the beasts to flee (Daniel 4:14). Under the full tree, it was a safe place to be.

Starved is the opposite of what the king describes. He says “its fruit was abundant, and upon it was food for all,” and that “from it every creature was fed.” Nobody leaves hungry from this tree. If anything, they leave looking for a nap.

The king never mentions silence. He talks about leaves, fruit, shelter, nests and food: “Under it the beasts of the field found shelter, in its branches the birds of the air nested, and from it every creature was fed.” It sounds like a busy tree to me. I think quiet was not what it was known for.

That's the order. The watcher calls out in a loud voice, “Cut down the tree and chop off its branches; strip off its leaves and scatter its fruit.” After that long description of a great tree, this is a hard turn. The watcher doesn't whisper it either.

The watcher says the opposite. He calls out, “Cut down the tree and chop off its branches; strip off its leaves and scatter its fruit.” The tree that reached the sky is not left alone. He even says to let the beasts flee from under it.

No second tree in this dream. The watcher says, “Cut down the tree and chop off its branches.” The only thing he leaves in the ground is the stump with its roots, which comes next (Daniel 4:15). So there's nothing about a neighbor tree.

Not this time. The watcher says to “leave the stump with its roots in the ground, with a band of iron and bronze around it, in the tender grass of the field.” The stump stays put. It gets a band around it, and it doesn't get pulled up.

False, and good catch. The watcher says, “But leave the stump with its roots in the ground, with a band of iron and bronze around it, in the tender grass of the field.” Everything above ground gets cut, but the roots stay. It's a tree that's chopped and still isn't finished.

explanations.answer: So the living know the Most High rules
explanations.explanation: That's the reason given. The decree is declared “…so that the living will know that the Most High rules over the kingdom of mankind and gives it to whom He wishes…” The holy ones state the purpose themselves. It's about who is really in charge.

explanations.answer: So the beasts have a place to graze
explanations.explanation: Grazing does show up in the dream, but it's not the reason. The reason is “…so that the living will know that the Most High rules over the kingdom of mankind and gives it to whom He wishes…” The beasts are just part of the picture. The point is about who rules.

explanations.answer: So the wise men stop their magic arts
explanations.explanation: The holy ones say nothing about the wise men or magic. Their reason is “…so that the living will know that the Most High rules over the kingdom of mankind and gives it to whom He wishes…” That's the whole purpose in their own words. It's bigger than any one room of experts.

explanations.answer: Don't let the dream alarm you
explanations.explanation: Right. Daniel, whom the king calls Belteshazzar, is perplexed, so the king says, “Belteshazzar, do not let the dream or its interpretation alarm you.” Here's the man who was alarmed by the dream, telling someone else not to be. I think that's a kind thing to say, even if it's a little funny.

explanations.answer: Hurry up and tell me right now
explanations.explanation: The king doesn't rush him. Daniel is perplexed for a time, and the king says, “Belteshazzar, do not let the dream or its interpretation alarm you.” That's an encouragement, not a deadline. Daniel gets room to answer.

Nobody gets sent home. When Daniel is perplexed, the king says, “Belteshazzar, do not let the dream or its interpretation alarm you.” Daniel answers right there. The king had waited long enough already.

Yes, enemies. Daniel says, “My lord, may the dream apply to those who hate you, and its interpretation to your enemies!” I think he's softening hard news before he says it. That's how it sounds to me, anyway.

Advisers aren't mentioned in Daniel's answer. He says, “may the dream apply to those who hate you, and its interpretation to your enemies!” He wishes it on the king's enemies, not on anybody close to him. The wise men had already failed, but he doesn't aim anything at them.

No sons in Daniel's words. He says, “may the dream apply to those who hate you, and its interpretation to your enemies!” That's a wish for the king's side, aimed away from him. I think Daniel is easing into a hard message.

Straight to his face. Daniel says, “you, O king, are that tree! For you have become great and strong; your greatness has grown to reach the sky, and your dominion extends to the ends of the earth.” The tree and the king match up point for point. Daniel doesn't dance around it.
Daniel isn't the tree. He says to the king, “you, O king, are that tree!” He's the one explaining the dream, not the one in it. The tree belongs to the man sitting on the throne.

The watcher is a different figure in the dream. The king saw him coming down from heaven (Daniel 4:13), and the watcher spoke about the tree. Daniel says, “you, O king, are that tree!” So the tree is the king himself.

True. Daniel says, “This is the interpretation, O king, and this is the decree that the Most High has issued against my lord the king.” He doesn't say it's his own idea or the stars' idea. He names the Most High as the one who issued it.

It's actually true. Daniel says, “this is the decree that the Most High has issued against my lord the king.” Daniel says exactly who issued it, and it's the Most High. He says it out loud to the king of Babylon.

Mankind is right. Daniel says, “You will be driven away from mankind, and your dwelling will be with the beasts of the field.” The king is going to be pushed out from among people. Quite a change for a man whose letter began by greeting the whole earth.
Grass, yes. Daniel says, “You will feed on grass like an ox and be drenched with the dew of heaven.” An ox, friend. I've had some rough days in my day, but I never had to graze.

Close, since the beasts do come into it. Daniel says, “You will be driven away from mankind, and your dwelling will be with the beasts of the field.” So he lives with them, but it's mankind he's driven away from. It's easy to mix the two.
Leaves belong to the dream tree, and they get stripped off it (Daniel 4:14). For the king, Daniel says, “You will feed on grass like an ox.” So the menu is grass. No leaves involved.

Heaven isn't what he's driven from. Daniel says, “You will be driven away from mankind,” and that he will be “drenched with the dew of heaven.” Heaven's dew falls on him, so he's under it, not away from it.

Kingdom, yes. Daniel says, “As for the command to leave the stump of the tree with its roots, your kingdom will be restored to you as soon as you acknowledge that Heaven rules.” The stump left in the ground is the promise inside the bad news. It's a small piece of hope.

Family isn't what Daniel says. He says the stump means “your kingdom will be restored to you as soon as you acknowledge that Heaven rules.” It's about the kingdom coming back. Nothing in his words is about the king's household.

Youth isn't on the list, friend. Daniel says, “your kingdom will be restored to you as soon as you acknowledge that Heaven rules.” That's what the stump and its roots stand for. I would have asked for the youth, though.

explanations.answer: Turn from sin and show mercy to the oppressed
explanations.explanation: That's the advice. Daniel says, “Break away from your sins by doing what is right, and from your iniquities by showing mercy to the oppressed. Perhaps there will be an extension of your prosperity.” He gives the king something to do, not just a warning. He gives it right to the king's face.

explanations.answer: Stay hidden in the palace until it all passes
explanations.explanation: Hiding isn't what Daniel says. His advice is, “Break away from your sins by doing what is right, and from your iniquities by showing mercy to the oppressed.” That's about doing something. It's the opposite of waiting it out.

explanations.answer: Build a great temple to the Most High God
explanations.explanation: Daniel doesn't mention a building. He says, “Break away from your sins by doing what is right, and from your iniquities by showing mercy to the oppressed.” His advice is about how the king lives. It's not about a project.

explanations.answer: He built it all by his own power
explanations.explanation: That's what he says. The king exclaims, “Is this not Babylon the Great, which I myself have built as a royal residence by the might of my power and for the glory of my majesty?” Count the "my" words in that sentence, friend. It's a lot of me for one rooftop.

explanations.answer: It was all a gift from the Most High
explanations.explanation: That's not what he says, and it's the opposite of his words. He says, “Is this not Babylon the Great, which I myself have built as a royal residence by the might of my power and for the glory of my majesty?” He gives himself the credit. Notice he says "I myself".

explanations.answer: It has grown too big for one king
explanations.explanation: He sees no such problem. The king says, “Is this not Babylon the Great, which I myself have built as a royal residence by the might of my power and for the glory of my majesty?” He's proud of it, not worried about it. It's a long way from where he started his letter.

True. The voice says, “It is decreed to you, King Nebuchadnezzar, that the kingdom has departed from you.” It comes while the words are still in his mouth. There's no pause between the boast and the answer.

It's actually true. The voice from heaven says, “It is decreed to you, King Nebuchadnezzar, that the kingdom has departed from you.” That comes right after his speech about Babylon. The voice says it plainly.
Not at all. The text says, “At that moment the sentence against Nebuchadnezzar was fulfilled.” Nothing is put off for twelve months. The twelve months were the wait before the roof (Daniel 4:29).
False, and you saw it. The text says, “At that moment the sentence against Nebuchadnezzar was fulfilled.” It happened right then, with no waiting. He had already had his twelve months.

explanations.answer: His sanity is restored to him
explanations.explanation: Yes. The king says, “at the end of those days I, Nebuchadnezzar, looked up to heaven, and my sanity was restored to me.” Then he praises the Most High. It starts with him looking up.

The watcher isn't in this part. The king says, “I, Nebuchadnezzar, looked up to heaven, and my sanity was restored to me.” The watcher spoke in the dream (Daniel 4:13). Here it's the king who looks up.

explanations.answer: Daniel finds him in the field
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say Daniel comes. The king says, “I, Nebuchadnezzar, looked up to heaven, and my sanity was restored to me.” It's about him looking up. Nobody else is named in the scene.
The opposite happens. The king says, “My advisers and nobles sought me out, and I was restored to my throne.” They come looking for him. He doesn't get left in the field.

False, and that's the good news. The king says, “My advisers and nobles sought me out, and I was restored to my throne, and surpassing greatness was added to me.” They came looking for him, and the throne is waiting. It's a very different ending from the one he walked into.

explanations.answer: Humble those who walk in pride
explanations.explanation: That's his closing line. The king says, “And He is able to humble those who walk in pride.” He's not guessing. He's speaking from what happened to him, and I think that's why it lands.

He doesn't say that. He says the King of heaven “is able to humble those who walk in pride.” He does say the Most High “lives forever” (Daniel 4:34), but that's about God, not kings. The last line is about humbling.
He doesn't say that about Babylon. The king says, “And He is able to humble those who walk in pride.” He had just lived through what it means. Babylon isn't the one being praised in this verse.
